events.text: There is a cairn on the pass now, by the old zelkova tree, and it is for you. Pedlars climbing out of the valley stop, add three stones, and say a few words to the hill: a safe road, no bandits, no rain on the salt. Nobody decided this. It simply started, the way moss starts. This evening a salt pedlar adds three stones and then, because nobody is looking, a fourth, and asks you to look after a sick wife.

choices.text: Walk beside the pedlar, unseen, all the way down the far side

effects.log: You keep pace in the trees, a weight the pedlar can feel and never see. Two bandits waiting at the ford look up the slope, see nothing at all, and decide very suddenly to wait somewhere else.

choices.text: Knock the fourth stone off. Three is the custom

effects.log: The stone rolls down the path and stops at the pedlar's straw sandals. The pedlar stares at it, then laughs out loud. "Fair," the pedlar says to the hill. "Three it is. But do remember her."

choices.text: Ignore it. You are not a god of roads

effects.log: The pedlar goes on down into the dusk. The cairn grows anyway. Customs, you learn, do not ask your permission.

events.text: Someone has tied cloth to the zelkova: five colours, blue and red and yellow and white and black, torn from skirts and sashes. Every spring and autumn the village climbs up with rice cakes and a jar of rice wine and a drum, and an old man in a horsehair hat reads a prayer to you that gets several of your habits wrong.

choices.text: Make the tree bloom out of season, once, at the prayer

effects.log: White flowers open on a zelkova in autumn. The old man drops the prayer. The drum stops. By the next spring, three villages are climbing the pass instead of one.

choices.text: Eat the rice cakes after they go home

effects.log: They are steamed with mugwort and very good. In the morning the plate is clean, and the village takes this as the deepest possible blessing.

choices.text: Let the wind take the cloth, gently, to see if they tie it again

effects.log: They tie it again the next week, more of it, and tighter. You are touched in a way you did not expect to be.

events.text: A hundred years on, the cairn is the height of a house and the zelkova has a roofed shrine at its foot with a painting inside: a great dim shape with two kind eyes, by a painter who never saw you. Pedlars still add three stones. None of them knows why. A child asks a grandmother what lives on the pass, and the grandmother says, "The one who keeps the road," with complete certainty.

choices.text: Look at the painting a long time

effects.log: It is wrong in every detail and right about the eyes. You decide you will be whatever is in that painting, for as long as anyone climbs this pass.

choices.text: Leave the child a smooth river stone on the cairn

effects.log: The child takes it home. That family keeps a smooth grey stone on its ancestral shelf for eleven generations and tells everyone exactly where it came from.

events.text: Frost in the sixth month. Then hail. Then snow on rice seedlings that were green the day before. The earth shakes three times in a season, and the oxen in the valley die of a fever one after another, so even the ploughing is gone. By autumn whole families are on your slopes, stripping the inner bark of the red pines to boil into gruel. They strip your trees bare. Some of them do not walk back down.

choices.text: Drive the deer and the wild boar down toward the village

effects.log: You move through the high forest for a week, slow and patient, and every deer and boar and pheasant on the mountain flows ahead of you down into the valley. The village eats meat in a year when the next county eats its seed grain.

choices.text: Show them the roots: arrowroot, bellflower, the wild yam under the oaks

ok.log: You scrape the leaf mould off the places you know until the villagers notice the pattern. Within a month the children know the mountain's larder better than their grandparents did.

fail.log: They find some roots, and some of what they find is the wrong root. Two of them are sick for days. They keep coming back anyway, because they have nowhere else to go.

choices.text: Let them take the bark. The trees will grow back. They will not

effects.log: You lie still and let the mountain be eaten. Your pines are white to the height of a man for a generation, like ghosts standing in rows.

events.text: The famine has its graves now, a whole slope of small mounds. One grave on your mountain is tended every year by an old woman who was a girl that winter. She tells the grave, loud enough for the trees, that the year of the summer snow was the year the mountain fed them.

choices.text: Bring a deer to the grave and lay it down, as you did then

effects.log: She sees the deer lying at the foot of the grave and sits down very slowly beside it and cries for a long time, but not from sadness.

choices.text: Stay hidden. Let her keep the memory her own way

effects.log: She finishes her words, pours a little wine on the grass, and goes home. Her granddaughter carries the jar. Her granddaughter is listening.

events.text: Children in the valley play a clapping game now, two by two, with a rhyme: snow in summer, bark for rice, the mountain walked and the deer ran twice. None of them knows it was ever true. A new frost comes this spring, lighter, and the old people look up at your slopes before they look anywhere else.

choices.text: Walk the forest again, before they need to ask

effects.log: The deer run down twice, just like the rhyme. The children cannot believe their luck. The old people can.

choices.text: Let them face this one themselves. They are stronger now

effects.log: They have granaries now, and relief grain from the county, and a hard-faced headman who learned from the last time. They come through it. You are prouder of that than of any deer.

events.text: The Guest has come to the village: the smallpox spirit, Mama, whom nobody dares call by its own name. Red cloth hangs over doorways. Nobody sweeps, nobody quarrels, nobody cooks anything with a strong smell, in case the Guest is offended. On the twelfth night a mudang plaits a horse out of straw, loads it with rice cakes and paper, and leads it to the edge of the village to send the Guest home. The horse is very small. The road out of the valley runs past you.
events.arc: The Guest on the Straw Horse

choices.text: Carry the straw horse over the pass yourself, carefully

effects.log: In the morning the straw horse is gone from the boundary stone, and its hoofprints, which it does not have, are found on the far side of the pass. The fever breaks in nine houses out of eleven.

choices.text: Keep well away. Even the great do not insult the Guest

effects.log: You wait on the far ridge with your eyes shut while something cold and courteous goes by on the road. When you open them, the straw horse has gone, and the village is very quiet.

choices.text: Stand across the road. The Guest may leave, but by another way

ok.log: Something on the road stops before you, considers, and takes the long way round, through the next three counties, at speed. Whatever you are, it did not care to argue.

fail.deathCause: the smallpox Guest, whose road you stood across
fail.log: The Guest does not go round. It goes through you.

events.text: A pock-marked woman with a scholar's calm face comes up the pass alone and sits on a rock facing your slope. "I was six," she says to the hill. "The year the Guest left on a horse no one could find. My mother said the mountain carried it. I became a physician because of that story. I have come to say that it is not true, and that I am grateful anyway."
events.arc: The Guest on the Straw Horse

choices.text: Let a single pine cone fall into her lap

effects.log: She looks at it for a long time, then puts it in her medicine box. She is buried with that box, forty years later, and the pine cone is still in it.

choices.text: Say nothing. Some debts are paid by being doubted

effects.log: She sits until dusk and goes down to her patients. In her notebooks, beside a method for the pox, there is a small drawing of a mountain.

events.text: The county magistrate has written to the capital about the thing on the mountain, and the capital has sent the chakho, the king's beast-hunters: twenty men in dark quilted coats, with spears, bows, and dogs that do not bark. Their captain, {npc}, is paid by the size of the kill and the order of the blow. You watch {him} kneel by a track you left in the snow and go very still. Then {he} lays a hand flat in it, and {his} whole hand fits in the print you left.

choices.text: Leave tracks that lead them in a circle for three days

ok.log: On the third evening they come back to their own campfire from the wrong side. {npc} sits down in front of it and laughs until the dogs look worried. "It is playing with us," {he} tells {his} men. "Write that I failed. I would rather fail alive."

fail.log: {npc} is not fooled for a moment. By the second day the dogs have your scent, the real one, and the hunt is coming straight up the ravine.

choices.text: Show yourself on the ridge at dawn, and wait

effects.log: Twenty men look up at once. Nobody draws a bow. The dogs lie down flat. {npc} takes off {his} felt hat, slowly, and the hunt goes back down the mountain without a word.

choices.text: Go to ground and let them search

effects.log: They search all winter. They find a wolf, a bear and a very surprised hermit. They do not find you. {npc} leaves in the spring, looking back over {his} shoulder the whole way.

events.text: {npc} comes back alone, years later, without dogs or men, and builds a hut at the foot of your mountain. {He} has left the king's service. {He} does not say why. In the evenings {he} sits outside the hut and cleans a spear {he} never uses, and talks to the slope about the beasts {he} has killed, one by one, as if reading a list of the dead.

choices.text: Come down at dusk and settle within sight of the hut

mem.note: came to lie by my hut

effects.log: {npc} stops talking. The two of you look at each other across the clearing until it is dark. In the morning the spear is gone. You find it later, driven into the earth by the cairn, with the iron broken off.

choices.text: Leave {him} to {his} list

effects.log: {He} talks to the slope every evening for years. You listen, mostly. The list gets shorter as {his} memory goes, and the last names on it are the first ones.

events.text: A young hunter in a dark quilted coat comes up the ravine with a new chakho troop, the old captain's own grandson, carrying the old captain's broken spear shaft as a charm. The troop has orders to kill the thing on the mountain. The grandson has other orders, given by a dying old man, which nobody else in the troop knows.

choices.text: Meet the grandson alone, at the cairn, and let the boy see you

effects.log: The boy goes back to the troop and leads them, very convincingly, up the wrong mountain for a month. The report to the capital says the beast is dead. You are, officially, a story now.

choices.text: Scatter the troop with a rockfall before anyone reaches you

ok.log: Half the ravine comes down between you and them. Nobody is hurt. Nobody comes back, either.

fail.log: The rocks fall late and wrong. An arrow finds you in the dust before you get clear. (-15 health)

events.text: Blue fires on the road below the pass: dokkaebi. A big shaggy one has caught a farmer walking home drunk and is insisting on wrestling. Dokkaebi always lose at wrestling, everybody knows that, but this farmer is very drunk and the dokkaebi is cheating. The farmer is losing. A lost wrestle with a dokkaebi means a year of bad luck, or a lost cow, or worse.

choices.text: Lean out of the dark right behind the dokkaebi

effects.log: The dokkaebi turns, looks up, and up, and lets go of the farmer, who wins by falling on it. The blue fires go out all at once. The farmer tells the village a dokkaebi let him win. The dokkaebi tells the other dokkaebi something else.

choices.text: Take the dokkaebi on yourself, for the fun of it

ok.log: It hooks at you, you lean, and it goes flying into a rice paddy. It comes up laughing and covered in mud. Dokkaebi respect nothing like a good throw.

fail.log: It cheats. You lose. It is the most delighted creature in three provinces and tells everyone, for a century.

choices.text: Watch. Humans should learn not to walk home drunk

effects.log: The farmer loses and wakes up in a ditch with a broom in place of a cow. Sobriety comes to one household in the valley that year.

events.text: A bowl of buckwheat jelly appears on the rock by the road every first full moon, with a jar of rice wine: the dokkaebi's tribute. Tonight the dokkaebi itself is sitting beside it, waiting for you. It wants a favour. A widow in the valley has been feeding it buckwheat jelly for years, and it has been paying her in gold, and now it is tired of her and wants to stop and is too polite to say so.

choices.text: Advise it to tell her the truth

effects.log: It goes off to tell her the truth. She gives it a bowl of jelly and a speech, and it comes back a month later, still visiting, still paying, and much happier. Some arrangements are love.

choices.text: Tell it to hang a horse skull over her gate and claim she did it

effects.log: Dokkaebi hate horse blood and horse skulls. It does it, flees in theatrical terror, and the widow keeps the gold and a fine story. Everyone wins, in the dokkaebi way.

choices.text: Eat the buckwheat jelly while it is talking

effects.log: It watches the bowl go down, outraged, and then laughs so hard the blue fires dance. You are, it decides, a real friend.

events.text: The village is raising new guardian posts at its gate: two great faces carved from chestnut trunks, bulging eyes and grinning teeth, to frighten off disease and bandits. The young carver has given one of them a face nobody has seen before, with eyes far too large, and when the elders asked what it was, {npc} pointed at your hill.
events.arc: The Faces at the Village Gate

choices.text: Go down at night and look your carved face in the eye

effects.log: The great prints in the mud around the post are found at dawn. {npc} stands among the elders, pale and enormously pleased, and is never again asked to justify anything.

choices.text: Send a wind that knocks the post crooked. Too proud a face

effects.log: The post leans. {npc} straightens it and carves the eyes smaller. Then, at night, {npc} carves them big again. You let it stand.

choices.text: Pay no attention. Wood rots

effects.log: It does rot, in a few years. But they carve it again, the same face, and again after that.

events.text: The guardian post is on its fourth carving. The village is a market town now, and the post stands by a wine shop. Travellers ask what the strange face is meant to be. The shopkeeper, who is the old carver's great-grandchild, has a long and very profitable story about it, about half of which is true.
events.arc: The Faces at the Village Gate

choices.text: Let the story grow. It costs you nothing

effects.log: The wine shop names a drink after you. It is sweet, strong and not as good as the story.

choices.text: Visit the town one night and correct a detail the shopkeeper got wrong

effects.log: The shopkeeper finds a message in the mud of the yard at dawn, in marks as wide as a plough. The story changes. Business doubles.

events.text: Rice-planting season, and the dure is out: every able man in the village in one long line knee-deep in the paddies, the farmers' band thumping and clanging at the edge to keep the rhythm. They have painted a new flag for the team. In the old days it said only AGRICULTURE IS THE GREAT FOUNDATION. Now there is something on it above the words, painted by someone with more feeling than skill. It is you.
events.arc: The Flag of the Work Team

choices.text: Send a cool cloud over the line at noon

effects.log: A single cloud parks itself over the long line of bent backs all afternoon and nowhere else. The band plays twice as loud. They finish the planting a day early.

choices.text: Watch the line from the hill. It is a fine thing to see

effects.log: The rhythm of it gets into you: gong, step, plant, gong. Years later you catch yourself moving to it.

choices.text: Frighten the next village's team, who are stealing water from this one

effects.log: The water thieves see your eyes in the irrigation ditch at dusk and leave their spades. The two villages are not friends for a generation. Your village is very proud of you.

events.text: The village flag is old and patched, and the work team carries it to a contest of flags at the county seat: the oldest flag bows to no one. Theirs has your shape on it, and the county's oldest village has an older flag. The rule is that the younger flag dips first. The village elders are muttering. Somebody looks at your mountain.
events.arc: The Flag of the Work Team

choices.text: Let the flag dip. Old is old

effects.log: It dips. The old village is gracious about it, and the two teams drink together until dawn. Some customs are worth more than winning.

choices.text: Send a wind that holds the flag up straight

effects.log: No one can make the flag dip; the pole will not bend. The old village dips theirs instead, with frightened faces. Your village tells it for a hundred years. The other one tells it differently.

events.text: The court has banned the cutting of pines on your mountain: they are for warships and palace beams. A warden has come with a ledger and a brush to number every tree, and today the warden's guards have caught a widow's son cutting one for a coffin. The punishment for a pine is a beating that can kill.

choices.text: Drop a dead pine across the road, so there is a fallen tree to account for

effects.log: The warden looks at the new-fallen tree, looks at the ledger, looks at the boy. "Wind," the warden writes, at last. "One pine, by the wind." The coffin is made.

choices.text: Stand up out of the trees where the warden can see you

effects.log: The warden drops the ledger. The guards drop the boy. The page for your slope in the forest register says, in a shaking hand, unsuitable for inspection.

choices.text: Leave it. The law is human

effects.log: The boy is beaten and lives. His mother buries her husband in a box of pine planks he stole from a ruined temple. Nobody numbers temples.

events.text: A wedding procession is crossing your pass: a groom on a white pony, a carved wooden goose carried in front for faithfulness, a red palanquin with the bride inside, bearers, musicians. Halfway up, the lead bearer sees your eyes in the mist and stops dead. Everyone stops. The goose-carrier is praying. Somebody whispers that it is bad luck past bearing to meet a great beast on a wedding road.

choices.text: Bow your head to them, so it is luck and not bad luck

effects.log: Your head lowers in the mist, slowly, like a guest at the table. The musicians, after a long moment, start to play. That couple has nine children and tells every one of them the mountain came to the wedding.

choices.text: Close your eyes and let them pass as if you were a rock

effects.log: They pass. The bride never knows. The lead bearer drinks a great deal at the feast and tells nobody, which costs a great effort.

choices.text: Ask for a toll, as the bandits do: the wedding cakes

effects.log: One low sound, and the cake boxes are set down on the path and the procession hurries on lighter. The cakes are excellent. The marriage, you hear later, is happy, but it starts with a story nobody tells the in-laws.

events.text: A brown cloud comes over the hills in the fifth month, and it is not rain. Locusts. The villagers run into the fields with gongs and burning straw, and the children with baskets, and none of it is enough. The rice is going in front of their eyes.

choices.text: Raise a wind off your mountain and drive the swarm out to sea

ok.log: You pull the air down off the peaks in one long cold rush. The swarm tears like paper and goes east, over the hills, out over the water. Half the harvest is saved. The village says the mountain exhaled.

fail.log: The wind comes, but it scatters the swarm into three valleys instead of one. Fewer locusts each. More villages hungry. No one blames you. You do.

choices.text: Eat them. All day

effects.log: It turns out you can eat a very great many locusts. The village watches you do it from the paddy dikes and does not know whether to cheer or pray.

choices.text: Let it pass. Swarms come and go

effects.log: It passes, and takes two thirds of the rice with it. The county sends relief grain in the winter, cut with chaff and sand.

events.text: At the five-day market a pedlar with cotton tassels on a felt hat is selling pieces of you: a bundle of coarse hair, a chip of grey stone, a vial of murky water. Each one cures fevers, brings sons and frightens bandits. They are selling very well. None of them are anything to do with you.

choices.text: Appear at the edge of the market and stare at the pedlar

effects.log: The crowd turns, follows the pedlar's gaze, and sees what the pedlar sees. The pedlar leaves without the stall. The market keeps the stall, and the vials, and sells them for twice the price.

choices.text: Leave a real gift at the stall: a stone you have rested on for a century

effects.log: The pedlar finds a warm grey stone at dawn among the fakes, the only one that is not, and never sells it. The pedlar's family keeps it on the shelf, and in time stops selling fakes altogether.

choices.text: Let them. If it comforts the sick, so be it

effects.log: Some of the sick get better, as some always do. The pedlar gets rich. You find you do not mind as much as you expected.

events.text: A baby in a hemp cloth, in a basket, at the foot of the oldest pine on your slope. Whoever left it knew the stories and hoped. The night will be cold. Down on the path a young monk with a begging bowl is walking toward the temple and will pass in an hour, if anything brings the monk this way.

choices.text: Curl around the tree all night and keep the cold off

effects.log: The baby sleeps warm against the warmth of you. At dawn you call the monk up the slope with a noise in the bushes, and stay just long enough to be seen. That child grows up at the temple, and is told about the night, and becomes a very famous monk with a very strange story.

choices.text: Carry the basket down and set it in the monk's path

effects.log: The monk finds a basket in the middle of the path where nothing was a moment before, and around it, pressed in the frost, prints too large to understand. The monk picks up the baby and does not look back.

choices.text: It is not yours to raise. Let the mountain decide

effects.log: The monk comes up the slope by chance, following a wild boar. Or so the monk thinks. You tell yourself you did nothing, and are not sure it is true.

events.text: The earth shakes in the night: once, then a long rolling second time that brings down roofs. Your own mountain groans under you, and you feel the whole wet face of the slope above the village begin, very slowly, to slide.

choices.text: Throw yourself across the slope and hold it

ok.log: You brace the whole weight of you against the moving earth, and for a long moment it is the mountain or you. It is you. In the morning the villagers see a new ridge of rock and soil curved above their roofs, the exact shape of something lying down. (-10 health)

fail.deathCause: a mountainside, held back for one night too long
fail.log: The mountain is heavier than you.

choices.text: Wake the village so they can run

effects.log: They run, half-dressed, into the paddies. The slope comes down behind them and buries a third of the houses and nobody in them.

choices.text: Save yourself

effects.log: You get clear of the slide. The village loses eleven people. They hold the funeral at your cairn and ask why the mountain did not warn them, and the question stays with you.

events.text: The charcoal burner's kiln on the north slope has cracked in the wind, and the fire is out and running uphill through dry pine, straight toward the old forest where you sleep. The charcoal burner is beating at it with a wet sack and has no chance at all.

choices.text: Call rain down onto the slope

ok.log: A black cloud folds down out of a clear sky onto one burning slope. The charcoal burner stands in the steam with the sack in both hands and does not move for an hour.

fail.log: The rain will not come for you yet. You fight it the hard way, throwing earth and rolling in ash, and it goes out at last with half the north slope black. (-10 health)

choices.text: Break a firebreak through the trees with your own weight

effects.log: You cut a gap through the pines that the fire cannot jump. In the morning there is a long bare scar across the mountain that the village calls your road. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go to the other side of the mountain and wait

effects.log: The fire burns itself out on the bare rock. You lose the forest you slept in for ages, and the charcoal burner loses the hut. You find another forest. The charcoal burner goes to another county and never burns charcoal again.

events.text: On the highest flat rock of your mountain, where nobody climbs, two old men in pale robes are playing baduk. They are not old men. A young woodcutter has wandered up and is sitting on a stump, watching the game with his mouth open, his axe across his knees. One of the players glances at you and says, without surprise, "Ah. You. Sit, if you like. This game has a while to go."

choices.text: Sit and watch the game

effects.log: White plays a stone. Black thinks. The light does not change, and changes, and does not change. When the game ends you look down: the woodcutter's axe handle has rotted to dust, and the woodcutter is grey-haired, and down in the valley the village has moved to the other bank of the river.

choices.text: Send the woodcutter home before it is too late

effects.log: You nudge the young man off the stump with a soft gust. He goes down the mountain dazed, with his axe whole, to a village that has only lost an afternoon. The players do not seem to mind. One of them says, "Kind. Slow, but kind."

choices.text: Ask them what they are playing for

effects.log: "For the sake of the game," says White. "For the next stone," says Black. You wait for a better answer. There is not one, and it takes you a long time to understand that there was never going to be.

events.text: The flat rock again, decades later. The board is there. The bowls of stones are there. The players are not. One stone lies by itself in the middle of the board, a white one, where no move was made when you watched.

choices.text: Play a black stone beside it

ok.log: The board is empty when you look again, and the bowls are gone, and something like laughter goes down the mountain on the wind. You feel, for a whole year after, as if you can see three moves ahead of the weather.

fail.log: You place it. Nothing happens. You wait a year, and it is still nothing. Some games are not open to everyone.

choices.text: Leave the board exactly as it is

effects.log: You never touch it. A hundred years later a hermit finds the rock and the board and the one white stone, and builds a hut there, and is happy all of a long life.

events.text: A bear on your mountain has crawled into a cave with a bundle of mugwort and twenty bulbs of garlic, because of a very old story: eat only these, see no sunlight for a hundred days, and you will wake up a human. It is day forty. It is very hungry. It is calling across the valley to you, because you are the only other thing on the mountain it can talk to, to ask whether it is worth it.

choices.text: "It is worth it. Finish"

effects.log: You bring it snow-water every night and stay awake with it, talking. On the hundredth day there is no bear in the cave. There is a young person in a bearskin, blinking at the sun, who walks down to the village and is never quite like the others there.

choices.text: "Being a bear is a fine thing. Come out"

effects.log: It comes out on day forty-one and eats an entire beehive. It is the happiest bear in the province for the rest of its life, and visits you every spring.

choices.text: "Ask yourself why you want to"

effects.log: It thinks about this for the rest of the hundred days. On the last one it walks out of the cave still a bear, and says it has decided something, and does not tell you what.

events.text: A family in the village has a strange custom: every first snow, they leave a bowl of mugwort rice cakes at the cave on your mountain and bow toward your slope. The eldest daughter, who has the family's broad shoulders and slow, dark eyes, says it is for a great-great-grandmother who came out of the mountain.

choices.text: Take the cakes and leave a honeycomb in return

effects.log: The family is delighted and not at all surprised. Honey, the daughter says, was always going to be the answer.

choices.text: Watch them from the trees, remembering

effects.log: Somewhere in you the long talks in the snow come back, word for word. Humans forget. You do not, and you are glad of it tonight.

events.text: First full moon of the year. The children fly kites from the hill and, at the end, cut the strings so the kites carry away the year's bad luck, with SEND MISFORTUNE AWAY painted on them. This year every cut kite drifts the same way, toward your peak. They land in your trees. Forty kites of a village's bad luck, all for you.
events.arc: The Kite on the First Full Moon

choices.text: Burn them on the peak where the village can see

effects.log: A small bright fire on the summit at midnight. Down in the village the old people nod: the mountain took it, the mountain burned it. They have a good year. Whether you had anything to do with that, you honestly do not know.

choices.text: Keep them. Read every one

effects.log: Bad luck, written by children: a sick grandmother, a lost dog, an older brother who hits, a father who drinks. You remember all forty. In the summer, some of them get better.

choices.text: Blow them back over the village

effects.log: Forty kites come down in the village square in the morning. The village has a very bad year, mostly from worrying about it.

events.text: A poor family's only ox has broken its rope and gone up your mountain, and the boy who was minding it is going up after it, crying, into the ravine where the village says nobody comes back. The ox is grazing quite happily in your meadow. The ox is worth more than the family's house.

choices.text: Walk the ox down to the boy

effects.log: The boy rounds a rock and sees the ox coming down the path with something large and calm following it. The boy sits down. The ox walks up and licks his face. Nobody in the village believes him, which he grows up not minding at all.

choices.text: Turn the ox toward home with a low sound, and stay hidden

effects.log: The ox comes trotting down the ravine with its eyes rolling and passes the boy at a gallop, headed straight for its stall. The boy follows it home and gets a beating anyway, for losing it.

choices.text: An ox in your meadow is an ox in your meadow

effects.log: The boy finds the rope and the nose ring. The family lives on borrowed oxen for years. The village stops letting its children near the ravine. That was, perhaps, what you wanted.

events.text: The farmers' band goes house to house at the first full moon, treading on the earth spirit in every yard to keep the year's luck in: gongs, drums, a lion mask, a song for each corner of each house. This year, for the first time, they finish the round at the foot of your mountain, and the lead gong player sings a verse to the slope, asking it to stay asleep and kind.

choices.text: Answer with a long low sound that shakes the gongs in their hands

effects.log: Every gong in the band rings by itself for a heartbeat. The band runs home in a mass, then comes back the next year with twice as many people, because now everyone wants to hear it.

choices.text: Stay asleep and kind, as asked

effects.log: You do. The village has an easy year. The verse to the mountain stays in the round forever after, the last song of the night.

events.text: You need to cross the great river, and the ferry is the old way. You make yourself as small as you can, a shadow in the dusk on the landing. The old ferryman looks at the shadow, looks at the boat, which is already sitting a hand lower in the water than it should, and says, "Fare is the same for everybody."

choices.text: Pay with a carp the size of a child, left on the landing

effects.log: The old man crosses with the boat almost under water, poling with great dignity, and does not say one word the whole way. On the far bank there is a carp. He eats well for a week and tells nobody, which is the real fare.

choices.text: Swim, and save the old man the trouble

effects.log: You go into the river and the river goes up the bank on both sides. The ferryman watches you cross and then spends the night bailing the boat.

choices.text: "Everybody does not weigh what I weigh"

effects.log: He takes you across for nothing, sweating, and asks you never to come back. You come back twice more in his lifetime. He charges you nothing each time and complains the whole way, and you look forward to it.

events.text: Three village boys have dared each other all the way up to the place where you lie. The bravest is creeping toward you with a stick, to touch the thing on the mountain and go home a hero. The other two are already halfway down the slope, in spirit.

choices.text: Let the stick touch you. Then open one eye

effects.log: The stick taps. The eye opens. Three boys reach the village in a time that is never beaten. The bravest one becomes a soldier, then a general, and says to the end of his life that nothing on any battlefield ever frightened him like an eye the size of a door.

choices.text: Close your eyes and let them think you are a rock

effects.log: They poke you, climb on you, and have a picnic on your back. You have rarely been so patient. They go home and tell everyone the beast is a lie, and the village children play on your mountain for a generation.

choices.text: Roar

effects.log: The roar goes down the valley and shakes the persimmons off the trees. Nobody climbs the mountain for years. It is very quiet. Quieter than you would like.

events.text: The village well has gone dry in a hot summer, and the women carrying water from the river are walking two hours each way with jars on their heads. You know where the water went. You have felt it moving under your mountain all spring, deeper and sideways, toward an old fault in the rock.

choices.text: Dig down to the vein and break it open on the slope above the village

effects.log: One night of digging, and in the morning a spring is running out of the hillside where none ever ran. The village builds a little roof over it and calls it the Mountain's Gift. The old well stays dry. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Push the water back toward the old well, slowly, underground

ok.log: It takes a month. Then one morning the bucket comes up full and the whole village shouts at once. Nobody knows why, and that is how you like it.

fail.log: The water goes where it wants. You lose it altogether for a season and have to dig it out again later, more carefully.

choices.text: Water goes where water goes

effects.log: The women carry it from the river for three summers until the rains come back. They curse the mountain while they walk. You hear every word.

events.text: Horsemen from the north have burned the great temple in the south, and with it the carved woodblocks of the whole Buddhist canon. The court has fled to an island, and from the island an order has come: carve it all again, every word, as a prayer to drive the invaders out. Monks are on your mountain, marking your white birches. The wood must soak in seawater for three years, boil in salt, dry three more in shade and wind. It is the work of a generation. The invaders' scouts are in the next valley.

choices.text: Guard the woodcutters while they work

effects.log: A scouting party comes over the ridge one dawn. It does not come down the other side. The monks finish the cutting in peace and float the logs to the sea, and the old abbot leaves a bowl of rice at the edge of the forest every evening until they are done.

choices.text: Show the monks the oldest, straightest birches, deep in your forest

effects.log: Trees no axe has touched in five hundred years, straight as bowstrings. The master carver weeps when the first one comes down. The blocks cut from that wood never warp.

choices.text: These are your trees. Drive them off

effects.log: The monks flee down the slope with their axes. They cut the birch on another mountain, two years later than they wanted. You keep your forest. The war goes on.

events.text: The birch logs from your mountain are still lying in a salt inlet on the coast, three years later, weighted down with stones. A storm is coming in off the sea, the kind that tears inlets open. The monks guarding them are three old men and a boy.

choices.text: Go to the coast and shelter the mouth of the inlet with your body

effects.log: The storm beats on you all night. In the morning every log is still in the inlet, and the three old men and the boy are kneeling on the shingle, facing a long dark shape that is already going back inland. (-12 health)

choices.text: Call the storm away, out to sea

ok.log: The black wall of it bends out over the water and breaks on an empty island. The monks never know how close it was.

fail.log: The storm comes in anyway. A third of the logs go out to sea. The rest are enough, just. The master carver adds one more line to the prayer.

events.text: The blocks are finished: eighty thousand of them, fifty million characters, carved by men who bowed three times before every character. They are kept now in long airy halls in a mountain temple, and on the end of one block, in a corner where nobody reads, a carver has cut a tiny shape that is meant to be you.

choices.text: Visit the hall at night, once, to see it

effects.log: The halls smell of birch and lacquer and salt. You find the block. You wait outside the hall until dawn, listening to the wind go through the slatted windows, through fifty million words, like a monk chanting very quietly forever.

choices.text: Leave it. Some things are better unseen

effects.log: You never go. But in the years when the war is worst you sometimes feel, very faintly, as if something far away is praying for you by name.

events.text: The temple below your ridge used to have two hundred monks and a bell you could hear from three valleys. Under the new dynasty the scholars at court despise monks; they are barred from the capital, and the county takes them for labour. This one has eleven monks left, and every one of them now spends the whole year beating paper mulberry into pulp for the government's paper tax. The bell has not been rung in a year. They cannot spare the hands.

choices.text: Ring the bell yourself at dawn

effects.log: The great bronze note rolls out over three valleys at dawn and every monk in the courtyard drops what they are holding. The old abbot looks up at the ridge and laughs for the first time in years. The bell rings every dawn after that, and nobody is ever seen ringing it.

choices.text: Strip the paper mulberry on your slopes in the night and leave it at the gate

effects.log: Bundles of bark at the temple gate every morning for a season, enough to meet the tax twice. The monks have their afternoons back. They spend them, as monks do, sitting very still.

choices.text: The quarrels of scholars and monks are not yours

effects.log: The temple goes on beating paper. Two of the eleven die of it that winter. You hear the bell, in your memory, for a long time after.

events.text: War. The country is overrun from the south, and the king has called on the monks to fight. The abbot of the temple below your ridge, a frail old man who has spent fifty years beating paper, is raising a band of monk-soldiers with staffs and farm tools, and he has come up the ridge path alone to ask the mountain whether he is doing a wicked thing.

choices.text: Give him a sign: lay a fallen tree across his path, pointing south

effects.log: He looks at the tree for a long time and goes back down. The monk band marches south in the spring and holds a mountain fortress for a winter. He does not come back. Some of the young ones do.

choices.text: Give him a sign: lay a fallen tree across his path, pointing home

effects.log: He nods slowly and goes back to the temple. He keeps it open as a hospital all through the war. Soldiers of both kings die in its courtyard, and every one of them is chanted for.

choices.text: Show yourself. Let him make his own choice, but not alone

effects.log: He sits with you on the ridge all night without speaking. At dawn he goes down and rings the bell, and the monks gather, and he tells them they must each choose, and that whatever they choose, the mountain saw them.

events.text: The temple is gone. The roof fell in a century ago. Where the courtyard was there is now a market every five days: pedlars, rice wine, a fortune teller, a man selling paper. The bell was melted down for coins in some war or other. Only the old stone lantern still stands, in the middle of the market, and people tie their donkeys to it.

choices.text: Ring the empty air at dawn, as you used to

effects.log: At dawn on market day a great bronze note sounds over the stalls from nowhere. The stallholders look at each other. An old paper seller, who had a grandfather who was a monk here, puts down the paper and cries.

choices.text: Walk through the market at night, among the empty stalls

effects.log: You find the place where the abbot used to sit. It is a noodle stall now. The ground there is still a little worn. You settle beside it until the roosters start.

choices.text: Let it be a market. Markets are good too

effects.log: Children chase each other round the old stone lantern. People argue about prices and fall in love. It is noisier than the temple ever was, and not less holy, you decide.

events.text: The court has built a beacon station on your peak: five round stone mounds in a row, a hut, and an old soldier called {npc} who must light them. One fire means all is well. Two, enemies sighted. Five, the enemy has landed and is fighting. Smoke by day, fire by night, peak to peak all the way to the capital. {npc} lights one fire every evening and talks to your mountain, because there is no one else up there to talk to.

choices.text: Keep the old soldier company on long nights

mem.note: kept me company on the peak

effects.log: {npc} gets used to the great warm darkness beyond the mounds. The talk gets longer. You learn about a dead spouse, a child in the capital, and the exact way to make wolf dung burn black.

choices.text: Keep your distance; a soldier with fires is a soldier with fires

effects.log: {npc} lights one fire a night and grows old on the peak. You hear every word, from a distance, for years.

events.text: Sails on the sea at dawn: hundreds of them. Then smoke on the coast where the port town is. {npc} is on the peak with a fever, shaking too hard to strike the flint, and the wind is blowing rain in off the sea. Five fires must be lit, now, or the capital will not know for a day.

choices.text: Light them yourself

ok.log: You take the flame from the little hut fire and carry it, with enormous care, to five wet mounds, one after another, and shelter each until it catches. Five columns of black smoke go up into the rain. On the next peak, a long way off, five answer.

fail.log: Three catch. Two drown. Three fires go up the line to the capital: enemies at the border. It takes another day for the truth to follow. A day is a great deal, in war.

choices.text: Hold off the rain over the peak while {npc} lights them

effects.log: The rain falls everywhere but the peak. {npc} lights the five fires with shaking hands, then sits down against the last mound and says, to you, "So you were listening all those years."

choices.text: Go down to the port and fight

ok.log: The landing party on the beach meets something it has no word for. It gets back in its boats. The beacon is lit late, by a feverish old soldier, and it says only two fires, because by then it is true.

fail.deathCause: an invading army on a beach, which had firelocks
fail.log: There are too many, and they have firelocks.

events.text: The beacon station is long abandoned: five tumbled stone mounds with grass on them. On the anniversary of the landing the people of the port climb your peak with offerings, and the youngest child lights one small fire on the first mound. One fire: all is well.

choices.text: Answer with five lights in the sky over the sea

effects.log: Five pale lights hang over the water for the length of a prayer. The children talk of nothing else for a year. The old people go home very quietly.

choices.text: Stay beside the one fire until it burns out, as the old keeper did

effects.log: The fire burns down to embers and the people go home. You stay. It is the first peaceful night on that peak in a very long time.

events.text: The spring festival is coming, the fifth day of the fifth month: swings, wrestling, washing hair in iris water. Before it the town climbs up to your pass to fetch the god down, and the god comes in a tree: a mudang dances into a trance and runs into the forest and seizes whatever young tree the spirit points to. This year the mudang runs straight into the forest, and keeps running, and stops face to face with you.
events.arc: The Sacred Tree Comes Down the Pass

choices.text: Turn your head toward a young maple

effects.log: The mudang follows your eyes, grips the maple, and screams for the drummers. They cut it, hang it with cloth, and carry it down the pass in a crowd. The festival is the best in living memory. The mudang never says what was in the forest.

choices.text: Let the mudang seize you instead

effects.log: The mudang grabs hold, eyes closed, of something vast and warm. The eyes open. A short silence. Then a very long scream, and a maple is chosen at random by someone else, and the mudang retires that year.

choices.text: Back away into the trees

effects.log: The mudang stands in the empty clearing, panting, then picks a tree, any tree. Nobody knows the difference. The mudang does.

events.text: The festival has grown. Ten thousand people, a wrestling ring, swings hung from the willows by the river, and a play in masks about a mountain spirit who comes down for the festival in disguise. People laugh at the mountain spirit in the play. It is a terrible drunkard. It is, you realise, you.
events.arc: The Sacred Tree Comes Down the Pass

choices.text: Come down in disguise and watch the play

effects.log: You stand at the back of the crowd as an old pedlar for an evening and laugh at yourself until you have to sit down. The mask is wrong about everything, and right about one thing, which you will not say.

choices.text: Send a little rain on the last night, as a blessing

effects.log: A warm shower on the burning of the sacred tree, then clear sky and stars. The masked players take it as approval. In the play, from that year, the drunkard spirit leaves in a little rain.

events.text: A ghost has been haunting the ford below your valley: a girl in white, with her hair down, who died unmarried and angry. Travellers who cross at night come out of the water raving, or do not come out. She looks at you across the river tonight, and she is not afraid of you. The dead rarely are.
events.arc: The Ghost in White at the Ford

choices.text: Cross to her and ask what she wants

effects.log: She wants what she was promised: a wedding, a house, a name on a tablet that someone bows to. She was going to be married in the autumn. She drowned in the spring. She wants you to understand that she is not wicked. She is owed.

choices.text: Stand in the ford every night so no one crosses near her

effects.log: For a year the ford is closed by something worse than a ghost. Travellers go round by the bridge, a day longer. Nobody drowns. She stands on the far side and watches you, every night, without blinking.

choices.text: Drive her out of the river

ok.log: She goes, screaming, into the reeds downstream, and haunts the next village. You have solved a problem by giving it to someone else.

fail.log: Her cold goes into you like a needle. You are ill for a year. She is still in the ford. (-12 health)

events.text: The mudang from the market town has heard about the ghost and has a remedy as old as ghosts: a wedding. Somewhere there is always a young man who died unmarried too. The mudang has found one, a drowned ferryman's son, and has set a wedding table on a rock by the ford with two cups, but the ghost will not come close while you are there. Or perhaps she will only come close if you are.
events.arc: The Ghost in White at the Ford

choices.text: Stay, and stand as the witness

effects.log: She comes up out of the river in white and stands by the table. Something else, a young man with wet hair, stands on the other side. The mudang sings. The two cups empty. In the morning the ford is only a ford, and two names are written side by side on a tablet in the shrine.

choices.text: Go away and give her the river to herself for the night

effects.log: You hear the drums from the next valley all night. In the morning the mudang is asleep against the rock and the cups are empty. The ford is quiet from then on.

events.text: The war with the northern horsemen is over, and the captives are coming home: women carried off to the north, ransomed for silver by their families or walking back on their own. The village does not want them. They are called a word that is not said in front of children. One of them, a girl of perhaps nineteen, has come up your stream alone at dawn, and is washing, and washing, as if water could make the village forget.

choices.text: Make the stream warm around her

effects.log: The water goes warm as bathwater around her, and only around her. She stops washing. She sits in it with her eyes shut for a long time. When she climbs out she walks back down to the village with her head up.

choices.text: Show yourself on the bank, so the village sees who watches over her

effects.log: The women on the bridge see it: the girl in the stream, and above her, something vast and patient watching from the bank like a guard dog. They do not say the word again. Not in that village.

choices.text: Leave her be. This is between her and them

effects.log: She washes until her hands are raw and goes away along the river road, not to the village. You never learn where.

events.text: The girl from the stream is a grandmother now, with a little herb shop by the bridge and a sharp tongue the whole valley is afraid of. Every spring, at dawn, she walks up your stream alone and sits in the water, warm or cold, and talks about the year to nobody in particular.

choices.text: Warm the water for her again

effects.log: "There you are," she says, as the water warms, as if you were late. She tells you about her shop, her grandchildren, a magistrate she outwitted, and a neighbour she has never forgiven. It is the best morning of your year.

choices.text: Lie in the reeds and listen

effects.log: She knows you are there. She tells the reeds that she is old now, and has been happy, and that it was not anyone's gift but her own. You agree with every word.

events.text: The herb shop by the bridge belongs to a great-granddaughter now, and the family has a custom: a daughter of the house washes in the mountain stream at dawn on the morning of her wedding. Nobody remembers why. They just say the water there is warm for the women of that family, and it is.

choices.text: Keep it warm for them, every one

effects.log: Generation after generation of brides, giggling or terrified, in a stream that is warm in the cold dawn. None of them know the girl who started it. You do.

choices.text: Let the custom be its own warmth now

effects.log: One spring you do not warm it. The bride gets in, gasps, and laughs, and the whole family laughs with her. It does not matter any more. It has become theirs.

events.text: A broom star has appeared in the east, sweeping the sky with its long pale broom of light, and the court's Office of Astronomy has sent two observers up to your peak with a bronze armillary sphere to record it, night by night, for the king. They are very cold and very serious and terrified of the mountain. A broom star means a dynasty sweeping out, or a plague, or a war. They argue in whispers about which.

choices.text: Keep the clouds off the peak for them, every night

effects.log: Forty clear nights in a row in the rainy season. Their record is the finest in the office's history. In the margin of the last page, very small, one of them has written: the mountain also watched.

choices.text: Watch the star yourself. It is a thing worth watching

effects.log: It hangs there for a month, burning without burning, and you feel it pulling at something in you, very faintly, the way the moon pulls water. You do not know what it means. Neither do the observers.

choices.text: Frighten them off the peak and have it to yourself

effects.log: They leave the armillary sphere and run. The court records the comet from the plain instead, worse. The sphere stays on your peak and turns green, and for centuries people climb up to look at it.

events.text: The broom star is back, the same one, after a human lifetime: you know its light. There are new observers on your peak with a newer sphere. One of them, very old, is the grandchild of one of the first two, and has brought the old record to compare.

choices.text: Clear the sky again, for old times' sake

effects.log: Clear nights, again, in the wrong season. The old astronomer looks up at the slope where you lie and bows, very formally, like one colleague to another.

choices.text: Watch it with them, close enough to be seen

effects.log: The young observers are too frightened to write. The old one writes steadily, every night, and the last entry says: the broom star, and the thing on the mountain, both returned. Neither did any harm.

events.text: Summer, and the village children are swimming in the deep pool below your rocks, where a man drowned three years ago and was never found. The drowned who are never mourned stay in the water and get lonely, and the lonely ones pull. A boy goes under in the middle of the pool and does not come up.

choices.text: Go into the water after him

ok.log: Cold hands, many more than two, wrapped round the boy's legs. You tear him loose and come up through the surface with him, and the pool boils, and the children on the rocks see far too much of you. The boy lives. The drowned man's bones come up with him, tangled in his legs, and are buried properly at last.

fail.log: The cold gets into you. You get the boy out, half drowned, but the thing in the pool keeps a piece of your strength for a year. (-15 health)

choices.text: Shout for the village

effects.log: Your shout brings every adult running. They pull the boy out on a rope, blue and alive. Nobody swims in that pool again until a mudang has held a rite there, which costs the village a whole pig.

choices.text: The river takes what it takes

effects.log: He does not come up. Now there are two in the pool. You hear them some nights, talking.

events.text: The invaders are burning the valley. Forty villagers, mostly women, children and the old, have fled up your mountain into the caves, the deep ones where you sometimes sleep. Soldiers with torches are climbing the goat path after them.

choices.text: Lie across the cave mouth

effects.log: The torches reach the ledge and stop. In the torchlight there is a wall that breathes. The soldiers back down the goat path one by one, very carefully, without turning their backs. The villagers live in your caves all winter.

choices.text: Lead the soldiers away up the mountain

ok.log: A great crashing up on the north face; the soldiers follow it for two days into the snow and come down with frostbite and a story. The caves are never found.

fail.log: They follow you, and they have bows. You lose them at last in the high crags with three arrows in you. The caves are safe. (-12 health)

choices.text: It is not your war

effects.log: You go deeper into the mountain. The soldiers find the caves. Some of the villagers escape higher. Later, the survivors leave nothing at your cairn for a generation, and you understand why.

events.text: The village has been rebuilt, and every year on the day the soldiers left, the families who hid in the caves climb up with a feast and eat it inside, by firelight, the way they ate that winter: millet, dried radish greens, one bowl of rice for the oldest. The children who were born that winter are grandparents now.

choices.text: Lie across the cave mouth again, so they feel safe

effects.log: They look out at the great dark shape across the mouth of the cave, and the grandparents nod to the children: yes, like that. Exactly like that.

choices.text: Leave them a deer at the cave mouth, for the feast

effects.log: Meat, in the cave of hungry memories. The feast becomes a happy one, after that. Some of the old ones are not sure that is right. Most are.

events.text: A gang of bandits has moved into the ravine on your north side, and they have painted you on the cliff: a crude great shape with burning eyes. They tell every caravan they rob that the beast of the mountain is their master, and that anyone who resists will be eaten. Your legend is doing their work for them, and doing it well.

choices.text: Go and stand behind the painting while they admire it

effects.log: They look up from the painting to the cliff top and see the real thing looking down at them. By dawn the ravine is empty except for a stolen ox, which you drive back to its village.

choices.text: Let them keep robbing. Fear of you keeps the valley safe from worse

effects.log: The valley has no other bandits for twenty years, and pays a toll on every cartload. It is cheaper than war. It is not cheap.

choices.text: Ruin their name: guide every caravan safely round the ravine

effects.log: For a year every caravan finds a fallen tree turning it onto the safe road. The bandits starve, then quarrel, then leave. Their painting stays on the cliff, and the pedlars bow to it.

events.text: The bandits' painting on the cliff is still there, weathered almost away. A new magistrate has ordered it scraped off as superstition. The pedlars who bow to it every morning have refused. The magistrate's men are standing at the foot of the cliff with chisels, looking up.

choices.text: Let a few stones fall near the chisels

effects.log: The men with chisels decide the cliff is unsafe, which is true. The magistrate writes it up as a matter of public safety. The painting stays.

choices.text: Let them scrape it. It was never you

effects.log: They scrape it away. The pedlars are furious. The next week someone paints it again, better, by night. It was never you, and it is, now.

events.text: A geomancer has walked your mountain for three days with a round compass and has found the perfect grave site: the place where the earth's energy pools like water, where a father buried there will make his sons ministers for nine generations. It is in the middle of your back. A rich family is coming up the slope with a coffin.

choices.text: Shrug, once, very gently

effects.log: The ground under the geomancer rises a hand's width and settles. The geomancer looks at the compass. The compass needle is spinning. The family buries their father on the next hill, and nobody becomes a minister, and you sleep comfortably.

choices.text: Allow it. One small grave

effects.log: They dig, bury, build a mound. Their sons do well, though not ministers. You carry a dead nobleman about with you for centuries, and grow quite fond of him.

choices.text: Lead the geomancer to a better site that is not you

ok.log: A spring, a slope, a bend of the river: you shift the signs until the compass agrees. The geomancer is thrilled. The family is thrilled. You are not under a grave.

fail.log: The geomancer is not fooled and comes straight back to your back, now certain it is the best site in the kingdom. You end up shrugging after all.

events.text: Drought, the worst in thirty years, and the village has given up asking politely. There is an older way: you insult the spirit of the mountain water so badly that it must send rain to wash the insult off. The magistrate himself stands by while the villagers throw a pig's head into your spring, then a dog's, then a great deal of very bad language.

choices.text: Be insulted. Send the rain

ok.log: You gather the clouds in a fury that is only half pretended, and it pours for three days, and the spring is washed clean and so is the valley. The villagers dance in the mud. The magistrate writes it up as a successful rite.

fail.log: You try. A thin rain falls for an hour. The magistrate orders a second pig's head. You find yourself developing very strong feelings about pigs.

choices.text: Take the heads out and leave them on the magistrate's gate

effects.log: The magistrate opens the gate in the morning and finds the pig and the dog looking at him. The rite is not repeated. The rain comes when it comes.

choices.text: Ignore it. Rain is not yours to sell for pig's heads

effects.log: The spring stinks for a month. The rain comes in its own time. The village is sure the rite worked, and does it again the next time, and the time after.

events.text: Drought again, a generation later, and up the slope comes the village with a pig's head on a pole, singing the insults their grandparents sang, word for word. They have learned it as a song. Some of the insults are very creative. The children are particularly enjoying it.

choices.text: Send the rain, and a little thunder for the children

effects.log: The thunder makes every child shriek with joy. The rain makes every grown-up weep. It is the best rite anyone can remember, and the song gets two new verses.

choices.text: Send the rain and keep the pig's head

effects.log: It rains. The head is gone from the spring by morning. The village takes this as the spirit accepting the offering, which, in a sense, it has.

events.text: A girl from the village has the spirit sickness: a fever no herb cures, dreams that are not dreams, and every night she walks up your mountain in her sleep. The old mudang following her says this is how it begins: a spirit has chosen her, and if she refuses it she will die, and if she accepts it she will be a mudang. The spirit she keeps walking toward, every night, is you.

choices.text: Meet her on the path and let her see you

effects.log: She wakes in front of you on the moonlit path, and is not afraid at all. The fever breaks that night. She becomes the most famous mudang in the province, and every gut she dances begins with a song to the mountain.

choices.text: Turn her gently back down the path every night until the fever leaves

effects.log: It takes a hundred nights. The fever goes. She marries a potter and has a perfectly ordinary life, and sometimes at night she stands at the door looking up at your mountain, not knowing what she misses.

choices.text: It is not you she wants. Stay away

ok.log: She stops walking up the mountain. Something else had chosen her after all, an old general's spirit from the shrine. She becomes a mudang of generals. You are relieved, and a little jealous.

fail.log: The fever does not break. She dies in the spring, still walking toward you in her sleep. The mudang says nothing to the mountain at the funeral, which says everything.

events.text: A county magistrate who was saved, as a boy, from something on your mountain he has never described, has had a stele put up at its foot: a granite slab on a stone base, carved in fine characters with your deeds. It is a very flattering stele. Half the deeds on it are someone else's, and one of them is a flood you caused.

choices.text: Leave a mark on the stele beside the flood, as a correction

effects.log: A deep gouge appears overnight beside one column of characters. Scholars argue about what it means for three hundred years. The magistrate understands at once, and is embarrassed, and is a better magistrate after it.

choices.text: Accept it. Every legend is half true

effects.log: People come from three counties to read it. Some of them come up the mountain afterwards to see the real thing, and are disappointed or terrified in roughly equal numbers.

events.text: The stele has fallen. The base cracked in a frost, and the slab lies face down in a field, and a family is using its smooth back to beat laundry on. Scholars come sometimes and pay the family to turn it over, and make rubbings, and argue about the gouge.

choices.text: Set it upright again in the night

effects.log: In the morning the stele is standing on its broken base, perfectly upright. The family is furious about the laundry. You leave them a fine flat stone in its place.

choices.text: Leave it. A laundry stone is an honest end for praise

effects.log: The washing gets done on your deeds for two hundred years, and the stone is worn smooth as silk. You find this more comforting than the words ever were.

events.text: A pilgrim is going round your mountain by full prostrations: three steps, kneel, forehead to the ground, rise, three steps. All the way round, ninety li of rock and root. It is a vow, for a sick child at home. The pilgrim's knees are bleeding through the padding, and there is a long way to go, and winter is coming.

choices.text: Clear the path ahead each night: roots, stones, thorns

effects.log: Every morning the path ahead is swept smooth as a temple floor. The pilgrim notices on the third morning, and kneels a little longer, and goes on. The circuit is finished before the snow.

choices.text: Stand in the path and stop the pilgrim

effects.log: The pilgrim looks up at you, a long time, and then bows to you, and goes around you on bleeding knees, very slowly, still bowing. You stand there feeling very small.

choices.text: Watch. A vow is a vow

effects.log: You watch the whole circuit from the ridge. It takes eighty days. On the last one, the pilgrim bows toward you, specifically you, though you never showed yourself. Some people simply know.

events.text: A worn stone path circles your mountain now, polished by the knees of pilgrims, with a little bow-shaped hollow every three steps. Sick children's parents walk it. The story is that the first pilgrim's child lived, and that the mountain swept the path. Both parts are true.

choices.text: Keep sweeping it for them

effects.log: You sweep the pilgrim's road for generations, a little every night. It is the most humble thing you do, and somehow the thing you are proudest of.

choices.text: Let them sweep it themselves now

effects.log: The temple below takes it over, with brooms and a rota and a great deal of arguing. The hollows go on deepening. It belongs to them now, as it should.

events.text: The county has found silver in your mountain, and the court wants it. Miners, mostly debtors and convicts, are digging a tunnel into your mountain by lamplight. You can feel every pick stroke, like a tooth being drilled. The overseer beats them when they are slow.

choices.text: Flood the tunnel gently and close the vein

effects.log: Water bursts into the workings one night from nowhere, cold and steady. Nobody is hurt; you saw to that. The mine is abandoned as cursed. The miners, freed, scatter across the province with the story.

choices.text: Let them dig, but warn them before every rockfall

effects.log: A low groan in the rock, every time, before the roof comes down. In a few years the mine kills nobody, which is unheard of. The miners leave rice at the tunnel mouth. The silver goes to the capital, and you carry a hole in you.

choices.text: Show yourself to the overseer, in the dark, alone

effects.log: The overseer comes out of the tunnel with white hair and never beats anyone again. The mine closes within the year. The court blames the overseer.

events.text: The old silver tunnel is a shrine now. The miners' descendants keep it: a little altar a few steps inside, oil lamps, a bowl of rice, and a painting of the miners' lamps going down into the dark with two great eyes waiting at the bottom. They believe the mountain saved their ancestors. They ask it, every year, to keep their sons out of mines.

choices.text: Grant it: keep the young ones home, somehow

effects.log: Every year a reason turns up: a good harvest, a cousin with a boat, a teacher in the next town. Not one son of that family goes down a mine for two hundred years. They are very sure why.

choices.text: Settle in the tunnel on the festival night, so they feel you there

effects.log: The lamps flicker as you settle in the dark. The old people smile. The children whisper. You find that you have become a household god without ever deciding to.

events.text: A sickness of the bowels is running through the valley: the people call it the rat sickness, because it feels like a rat climbing up the legs into the belly, and they hang pictures of cats on their gates to frighten it. It began at the lower well. You can taste it in the water from your mountain: something wrong, downstream of the burial ground.

choices.text: Foul the lower well so badly that no one will drink from it

effects.log: One night the lower well stinks of rot and sulphur. Nobody will go near it. The village drinks from the spring on your slope instead. The sickness stops in a fortnight, and nobody ever knows why.

choices.text: Show the mudang the burial ground, and the stream under it

ok.log: The mudang follows a strange light down to the burial ground at night, and sees the seep, and understands. The graves are moved up the hill. The well is cleaned. The mudang gets the credit, which is fine.

fail.log: The mudang sees the light, decides it is the rat spirit, and holds a very loud rite at the burial ground. Half the village drinks the water there afterwards, for luck. It is a bad month.

choices.text: The sickness is not yours to fight

effects.log: It burns through the valley and out again by the first frost. A fifth of the village goes into the ground. The cat pictures stay on the gates for a generation.

events.text: The village has known about you for generations: the cairn, the rites, the stories. What it has never had is an answer. This morning, at the spring rite, when the village head finishes the old prayer and says, as the prayer has always said, "Hear us, honoured one," you decide, for the first time, to answer. You say: "I hear you." Three hundred people stop breathing.

choices.text: "I have always heard you. Go on"

effects.log: The village head, an old man with a pipe, lets the pipe fall and then picks it up and, with tremendous courage, goes on with the prayer. It is the strangest rite in the history of the valley. Nobody leaves until sunset.

choices.text: "Then listen, for once." Tell them what you have seen

effects.log: You tell them about their grandparents, about a flood they forgot, about a feud that began over a misplaced ox. When you stop, half of them are laughing and half crying. Two families end a feud on the spot.

choices.text: Say nothing more. Let them argue whether they heard it

effects.log: They argue for a generation. The ones who heard it never doubt. The ones who did not, never quite stop wondering. It is perhaps the most powerful thing you have ever said.

events.text: Now that you have answered, they come to ask. Every week: lost cows, marriages, sick children, boundary stones. One morning there are eleven people at your cairn before dawn, each with a question, each certain theirs is the most important, and a twelfth selling them rice cakes.

choices.text: Answer all of them, patiently, one by one

effects.log: It takes all day. The cow is in the east ravine. The marriage is a bad idea. The child needs boiled water, not talismans. The boundary stone was moved, by the asker. The rice cake seller makes a fortune.

choices.text: Answer one question a year, and let them choose which

effects.log: The village forms a council to choose the year's question. It meets for months. They learn more from arguing about what to ask than from any answer you give.

choices.text: Stop talking for a hundred years

effects.log: Silence again. The questions stop after a decade. Then, slowly, the villagers start answering each other.

events.text: A new county magistrate, young, Confucian, hard as a bamboo rod, has arrived with orders: the forest on your mountain is to be cleared for fields, the cairn torn down, the rites stopped as superstition. {npc} comes up to the cairn with forty woodcutters to start the work in person, and finds two eyes in the trees, at the height of {his} own, and a voice: "Magistrate. Before you cut, talk to me."
events.arc: The Magistrate Who Came to Clear the Forest

choices.text: Argue as a scholar would: the forest holds the slope that holds the town

mem.note: argued with me like a scholar

ok.log: You quote the classics on water and hills. {npc} quotes back. It goes on until dark. In the end {npc} sends the woodcutters home and writes to the capital that the forest is a necessary embankment, which is true, and which saves {his} face.

fail.log: {npc} is a better scholar than you. You lose the argument. The lower forest is cut. The cairn stays, as a concession {npc} will not explain to anyone.

choices.text: "Cut one tree. Then see what the mountain does"

effects.log: One tree falls. The ground shivers under forty pairs of feet. The woodcutters drop their axes and run. {npc} stands alone, white-faced, and does not run, and you respect {him} for it.

choices.text: "Clear the lower slope. Leave the old forest. Both of us can live with that"

effects.log: {npc} thinks, then nods once. New fields on the lower slope, and the old forest left standing above them. The harvests are good. The rites go on, quietly, and {npc} pretends not to know.

events.text: {npc} has been recalled to the capital, promoted, and has come up the mountain alone the night before leaving. "I came here to end you," {npc} says. "I am leaving with my mind changed about several things, and I do not care for it. Tell me one thing to take to court."
events.arc: The Magistrate Who Came to Clear the Forest

choices.text: "Rulers are mountains to the people. Be a forest, not a cliff"

mem.note: gave me a word for the court

effects.log: {npc} writes it on a fan. Decades later, a minister now, {npc} still has the fan, and the court has several fewer cliffs in it than it might have had.

choices.text: "Come back when you are old, and tell me if you kept it"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, the first time you have heard that. "Agreed," {npc} says. "Do not die."

events.text: An old official in plain clothes is carried up the path in a sedan chair and gets out at the cairn with a stick. It is {npc}, retired, very old. "I said I would come back," {npc} says. "I kept most of it. I would like to sit here a while."
events.arc: The Magistrate Who Came to Clear the Forest

choices.text: Sit with {npc} through the afternoon and talk about the years

effects.npcPass: old age, in the capital, a year after the visit
effects.log: Purges, famines, one good law that stuck. {npc} tells it all plainly. At sunset {npc} gets up and bows to the trees, and the trees, with a little help, bow back.

choices.text: Ask what {npc} failed at

effects.npcPass: old age, in the capital, a year after the visit
effects.log: It takes a long time to answer. The answer is honest and terrible and short. You tell {npc} it was still a life worth living. {npc} does not quite believe it, and is grateful anyway.

events.text: An envoy from a great sect has come up the mountain in white and gold, with gifts: silk, ginseng, a jade tablet. {npc} bows very correctly and says the sect's patriarch has heard of your wisdom, and would be honoured if you came to live in the sect's sacred lake, as its guardian, with every comfort. {npc} does not mention that the patriarch's cauldron is the size of a house, or that a great beast's inner core is the finest elixir in the world. {npc} does not need to.
events.arc: The Sect That Wants Your Core

choices.text: "Tell your patriarch I know what the cauldron is for"

effects.log: {npc} keeps a perfect smile and leaves the gifts. The smile goes on all the way down the mountain. It is still there, you suspect, when {npc} reports to the patriarch that the beast will have to be taken.

choices.text: Ask {npc}, quietly, whether {npc} wants to be part of this

ok.log: The smile cracks. {npc} sits down on the cairn and talks for an hour: a poor family, a debt to the sect, an elder who will not let go. When {npc} leaves, it is with a promise to warn you, if it comes to that.

fail.log: {npc} looks at you as if you have said something in very bad taste, and leaves.

choices.text: Eat the ginseng in front of {npc}, all of it

effects.log: It is very fine ginseng. {npc} watches a hundred years of root go into you in three mouthfuls and goes down the mountain to tell the patriarch the price has just gone up.

events.text: They come at the new moon: thirty disciples with chains written all over in cinnabar talismans, an array of flags around the mountain to bind you, and an elder with a jade sword who has killed beasts before. The array is closing. You can feel it, like a net drawn tight.
events.arc: The Sect That Wants Your Core

choices.text: Break the array at its weakest flag before it closes

ok.log: You find the flag where the weakest disciple stands and burst through it like a landslide. The array tears. The chains fall slack. The elder with the jade sword is the last to run, and runs fastest.

fail.deathCause: a sect's binding array and a jade sword, for the core inside you
fail.log: The array holds.

choices.text: Go deep into the mountain where no array can follow, and wait

effects.log: You go down into the roots of the mountain, past water, past dark. They hold the array for forty days and nights. Then the funds run out, and the disciples go home grumbling, and you come up into the spring.

choices.text: Call the storm down on the flags

ok.log: Lightning finds every flag pole on the mountain, one by one, like a teacher marking errors. The array is ash by midnight.

fail.log: The storm comes, and the talismans drink it. You tear free at last, but with a chain's burn across you that will ache for a century. (-15 health)

events.text: Word comes up the mountain with a pedlar: the sect that hunted you has fallen. A rival burned its halls; its patriarch died in a cauldron accident nobody believes was an accident. A gaunt survivor is at your cairn, a former disciple with nothing left, asking for shelter from the people who are now hunting them.
events.arc: The Sect That Wants Your Core

choices.text: Shelter the survivor

effects.log: The former disciple lives in a hut by your cairn for years, sweeping it, and teaching the village children to read. Hunted by the hunters' enemies, guarded by the hunted. The world is strange, and sometimes kind.

choices.text: "Your sect came for me with chains. Go"
