effects.log: The former disciple bows and goes. You do not watch which way. It is justice, of a kind. It does not feel like much.

events.text: The kingdom has been invaded from the sea, the king has fled north, the army is broken. A scholar from the valley, {npc}, has raised a righteous army instead: farmers, slaves, monks, a butcher, three hundred people with spears and sickles. {npc} climbs to your cairn at night, with mud on {his} robe. "I am a scholar," {npc} says. "I know nothing of war. You have watched a thousand years of it. Teach me."

choices.text: Teach the mountains: every path, cave and ford for ten days' march

effects.log: All night, path by path. {npc} draws it on silk with a shaking brush. That map wins eleven ambushes. The invaders never learn to fear the army. They learn to fear the hills.

choices.text: "Do not fight them. Hide the people"

effects.log: {npc} is silent a long time. Then {npc} turns the army into a column of refugees and leads three villages into the high valleys. Fewer heroes. Many more grandchildren.

choices.text: "I will fight with you"

ok.log: The invaders' camp at the ford wakes to something coming out of the river fog that is not on any of their maps. The righteous army goes in behind it. By morning the ford is theirs, and a story is born that will be told for five hundred years.

fail.deathCause: an invaders' volley at the ford, fighting beside a righteous army
fail.log: The firelocks of the invaders are not afraid of legends.

events.text: The war is over. {npc} is not rewarded by the court; {npc} is arrested, because a scholar who can raise an army is a scholar who might raise one against the king. {npc}'s family comes to your cairn: an execution is set for the spring.

choices.text: Go to the capital road and stop the prison cart

ok.log: The escort sees what is lying across the road and remembers urgent business elsewhere. {npc} walks out of the cart and into the hills and lives under another name for years.

fail.log: The cart takes another road. You arrive too late. The court records a monster seen on the capital road, and a scholar who died calmly.

choices.text: Send a dream to the king: the hills remember who saved them

ok.log: The king wakes sweating and pardons {npc} before breakfast, and never says why. {npc} goes home and teaches in a village school and never raises anything again but children.

fail.log: The king dreams of mountains and wakes afraid of them, and the execution goes ahead. {npc} dies facing south, toward home.

choices.text: "It is the way of kings. I cannot fight every one"

effects.log: {npc} dies in the spring. The family takes the map on silk home and keeps it in a lacquer box, and does not come to your cairn again.

events.text: Two hundred years on, the righteous army is a song. Schoolchildren learn it. There is a shrine in the valley to the scholar who raised it, and on the shrine's painted wall, behind the scholar on a ridge, is the dim shape of something vast. The song has a verse about the mountain. The song gets the mountain wrong.

choices.text: Visit the shrine and listen to the song once

effects.log: You wait outside the shrine wall while the children sing. They sing about a scholar who never knew fear, which is not true, and a mountain that roared, which you did not. It does not matter. It is a good song.

choices.text: Teach one child the true verse, in a dream

effects.log: The child wakes and sings it at breakfast: a scholar with mud on the robe, frightened, asking for help in the dark. The family is puzzled. The verse spreads anyway. Truth sometimes does.

events.text: A young scholar who failed the state examination has come to your cairn with an ink stone and an empty bound book. {npc} has heard that the mountain speaks. {npc} wants to write down everything you say, every word, for a book. "Not for the examiners," {npc} says. "For after we are all dead. Someone should keep it."
events.arc: The Book of the Mountain's Words

choices.text: Speak for a whole summer: history, weather, human folly

mem.note: gave me a summer of words

effects.log: Three books, then four. {npc} goes home in autumn thin and burning with it. The book is copied, and copied again, and in some provinces it is banned, which makes it far more popular.

choices.text: "Write down nothing. Listen instead"

effects.log: {npc} is horrified, then sulky, then, after a month, quiet. When {npc} leaves, the book is still empty, and {npc} is a different person, and better, and slightly annoyed about it.

choices.text: Dictate a book of lies, to see if anyone notices

effects.log: Nine-headed pheasants. Rivers that run uphill on festival days. A recipe for rice cakes that requires the moon. {npc} writes it all down with a straight face. It becomes the most beloved book in the kingdom.

events.text: A copy of the book comes back to you, a century later, carried up by a young reader with a worn copy under one arm. It has been copied so many times that half of it is now other people's ideas. There is a chapter about a war that had not happened when you spoke. The reader wants to know which parts are really you.
events.arc: The Book of the Mountain's Words

choices.text: "All of it. That is what happens to words"

effects.log: The reader thinks about this all the way down the mountain and becomes a copyist, and adds a chapter of their own, very carefully, at the end.

choices.text: Mark the parts that are yours with a press of a stone

effects.log: A third of the book, it turns out. The reader takes the marked copy home, and it becomes the true edition, and the scholars fight over it for three hundred years.

events.text: A mudang from the market town has climbed up with a blank silk scroll. {npc} serves the spirits of a mountain shrine: a general, a grandmother, a mountain god with a white beard on a painted scroll. {npc} wants to paint a new one, and make you the shrine's chief spirit. "You would come down when I call," {npc} says. "Into me. And speak."
events.arc: The Shrine That Wants Your Name

choices.text: "Paint me. I will come when it matters"

effects.log: The painting {npc} makes is nothing like you and exactly right. When it matters, which is three times in a few years, {npc} dances, and something vast looks out of {npc}'s eyes, and the town listens.

choices.text: "I come into no one"

effects.log: {npc} is not offended. "Most of the spirits say that at first," {npc} says, and leaves the blank scroll on the cairn for you to think about.

choices.text: "Paint me, but never call me. Speak in my name and I will know"

effects.log: {npc} agrees, and keeps the agreement, nearly. In a few years {npc} speaks in your name only once, to stop a lynching. You let that one pass.

events.text: {npc} is old and dying and the town is quarrelling over the shrine: who gets the drums, the costumes, the painted scroll of you. A grasping nephew wants to sell it to a collector. A young apprentice wants to keep the shrine. {npc} has asked that you settle it.
events.arc: The Shrine That Wants Your Name

choices.text: Come down into the apprentice at the funeral, once

effects.log: At the funeral gut the apprentice goes still, and something looks out of those young eyes, and says one sentence to the nephew. The nephew leaves town. The scroll stays in the shrine for two hundred years.

choices.text: Let them sort it out. Shrines are human things

effects.log: The nephew sells the scroll. The apprentice paints a new one, worse and more loving. You prefer the second, privately.

events.text: Two families have fought for three generations over a boundary stone between their paddies. The magistrate's court has ruled four times, for each side twice. The village compact has failed. Now both families have climbed to your cairn together, glaring, to ask the mountain where the stone really stood. You remember. You watched the great-grandfather of one of them move it, one night, a hand's width a year.

choices.text: Tell them the truth, all of it

effects.log: Silence. Then one family turns red to the ears, and the other bursts out laughing, a terrible, gleeful laugh. The stone is moved back. The families do not speak for a generation, and then their grandchildren marry, out of pure spite.

choices.text: "Split the strip and plant a tree on it"

effects.log: Neither is happy. Both accept, because a mountain said it. The persimmon tree grows on the boundary for three hundred years and both families harvest it, carefully, from their own side.

choices.text: "Your great-grandfathers settled this. Ask them"

effects.log: They go home and hold rites to their ancestors, and the dreams that come are inconclusive. The quarrel goes on, but more quietly, and with a certain nervousness.

events.text: Word has got about. The mountain judges. Now the cases come every month: a stolen pig, a broken engagement, a son who struck his father, a widow cheated of her field. The magistrate's court is empty. The magistrate is not pleased, and has sent a clerk to watch.

choices.text: Judge every case, fairly, and send the clerk home with the records

effects.log: The clerk copies your judgements for a year. The magistrate reads them and, grumbling, starts using them. The county becomes known for fair courts, and nobody but the clerk knows why.

choices.text: Send every case back down to the magistrate

effects.log: "The law is a human road," you tell them. "Walk it." They do, grumbling, and the magistrate, embarrassed, starts doing a better job.

choices.text: Judge only the cases the court got wrong

effects.log: A court of appeal on a mountainside. The magistrate is furious, then careful, then good. Fear of being overturned by a mountain is, it turns out, a powerful teacher.

events.text: An old man with a gourd of wine has walked up your mountain on the clouds instead of the path, sat down on your peak and offered you his company. He is a wandering immortal, eight hundred years old and drunk for most of them. "You have the look," he says, "of a beast that will reach heaven, if it stops caring what the villages think. Come travelling with me. Leave all this."

choices.text: "The villages are why I want to reach heaven at all"

effects.log: He looks at you over the gourd for a long time. "Hm," he says. "That is a harder road. Also a better one, possibly. I would not know." He leaves the gourd on your peak.

choices.text: Go travelling with him for a decade

effects.log: Ten years of clouds and tea and arguments on mountaintops. You come home wiser and very slightly cloud-headed, to find the village has had three new headmen and assumed you were dead.

choices.text: Sit with him and say nothing

effects.log: You sit. He drinks. The sun goes down. He tells you nine stories, three of them true. In the morning he is gone, and the gourd is full again.

events.text: The immortal is back, sober for once, and serious. "The sky is watching you now," he says. "Not kindly or unkindly. It watches everything that might rise. I came to tell you one thing nobody told me. Whatever you become up there, keep one human face in your memory. Just one. Hold on to it."

choices.text: Choose a face: the first human who was kind to you

effects.log: You find it at once: a face you have not thought of in centuries. It is still clear. The immortal nods, and drinks, and is gone. You keep it, as he said.

choices.text: "Why only one?"

effects.log: "Because you will forget the rest," he says. "I did. I cannot remember my mother's face. Do not let that happen to you." It is the only time you see him without the gourd.

events.text: A runaway slave from a great house in the county has hidden among the roots where you rest, not knowing what the roots belong to. Slave catchers with torches are working up the slope. {npc} has a name in the household register, a brand, and a family still in bondage. When you speak, {npc} nearly dies of fright, and then, astonishingly, asks for help.

choices.text: Hide {npc} until the catchers give up

effects.log: The catchers search the slope until dawn and find nothing but a very large rock, which they do not look at closely. {npc} walks over the mountain the next night to a fishing village where nobody asks about registers.

choices.text: Frighten the catchers so badly they never come up this mountain again

effects.log: The torches go out one by one, dropped. Your mountain becomes the place runaways head for, the place catchers do not go. Over the years, many come. You hide them all.

choices.text: "I cannot stop a law. But I can show you the road north"

effects.log: You tell {npc} every path and spring for three provinces. {npc} memorises them, trembling, and goes. You never learn if {npc} got there.

events.text: The household registers have been burned. A reform at court, a fire in the county office that may not have been an accident: the slaves of the county are free. An old fisher comes up the mountain with grandchildren to see the place among the roots. It is {npc}.

choices.text: "You came back"

effects.log: {npc} shows the grandchildren the hollow in the roots. "Here," {npc} says. "This is where I was born the second time." The children are unimpressed by the roots and very impressed by you.

choices.text: Ask about the family left in bondage

effects.log: {npc} found them, years later, and bought two of them free with fish money. The third had died. {npc} tells it plainly, and then weeps, all at once, for the first time in forty years.

events.text: Two armies have drawn up in the valley below you: a rebel lord's and the king's. Tomorrow they will fight in your rice fields, among your villages, in your river. Tonight, under a white flag, both generals have climbed to your cairn, each to ask the mountain's blessing, and found each other there.

choices.text: "Fight somewhere else. Not in my valley"

effects.log: They look at each other, then at you. In the morning both armies march two days east, grumbling, and fight on a bare plain where nobody lives. Your valley loses nothing but a few chickens to foragers.

choices.text: "Talk. You have both already climbed the same mountain"

ok.log: They talk until dawn, at first only to you, then to each other. There is no battle. There is a treaty, and a marriage, and twenty years of uneasy peace. The treaty stone stands by your cairn.

fail.log: They talk, and it goes badly, and they go down the mountain angrier than they came. The battle is the worst in a generation. You watch all of it.

choices.text: Bless neither, and watch

effects.log: The battle is fought in your fields. The river runs red as far as the sea. You learn the faces of the dead, because someone should.

events.text: The grandchildren of both armies plough the valley now, side by side. A farmer turns up a rusted spearhead, then a helmet, then bones. The village argues whether to bury them as the king's men or the rebel's. Nobody can tell. They come up to your cairn to ask.

choices.text: "Bury them together. They were all from this valley"

effects.log: One mound, one rite, one stone with no side carved on it. Every spring after, the whole village climbs to it together, whichever side their grandfathers fought on.

choices.text: Tell them which bones are which, exactly

effects.log: You remember every one. Two mounds, then. The village is impressed and a little frightened by how well you remember.

events.text: A royal envoy has come from the capital with a palanquin, musicians and an edict sealed in red: the king invites the honoured spirit of the mountain to the palace, to advise the throne, and to be given a title and a shrine in the palace garden. {npc} reads it aloud at your cairn, very formally, and then, very quietly, adds: "Please say no. The court will eat you alive."

choices.text: Say no, with great courtesy

effects.log: You compose a refusal in the high style and {npc} writes it down, grinning behind the brush. The king is offended for a month and then has it carved on a screen. The court thinks you very wise. You are only listening to an envoy.

choices.text: Go to the capital, for one season

ok.log: A season in the palace garden, advising a nervous king and outwitting four ministers. You stop one bad war and start one good school. You come home very tired and determined never to go back.

fail.log: The court is exactly as {npc} said. A minister tries to poison the shrine offerings in the second month. You leave in the night over the palace wall, which is not dignified. (-15 health)

choices.text: "Tell the king the mountain is the throne's best advisor where it stands"

effects.log: It becomes a saying at court: the mountain advises where it stands. Kings send questions up by envoy for a century. {npc} carries most of them.

events.text: {npc} comes up the mountain again, older, without a retinue: out of favour, dismissed, travelling home to the provinces. "I told you the court would eat you," {npc} says. "I forgot to say it would eat me too. May I sit?"

choices.text: "Sit. Stay as long as you like"

mem.note: let me sit when I had nothing

effects.log: {npc} stays a year, and writes poems, and gets better. The poems are the best thing {npc} ever does. The court reads them later, and is ashamed, for about a week.

choices.text: Tell {npc} where the king went wrong, so the next envoy knows

effects.log: {npc} writes it all down and sends it, in secret, to a young official {npc} trusts. Twenty years later that official is chief minister. Some of it takes.

events.text: A bandit chief with a hundred followers has come to your cairn alone, which takes nerve. "I am told you are the power in these hills," {npc} says. "So am I. Let us agree. I leave your villages alone. You leave my roads alone. Everyone else is fair game."

choices.text: "Everyone else is somebody's village"

effects.log: {npc} hears the weight in it. The band moves on to another province within the month. It is not a victory. It is somebody else's problem now.

choices.text: "Agreed. But if you break it, I will know"

effects.log: For years your villages are the safest in the kingdom and the roads around them the most dangerous. You are not sure you like who you have become for that.

choices.text: "Or you could stop, and farm the high valley I will show you"

ok.log: {npc} laughs, then stops laughing. The high valley is good land. Half the band goes with {npc}. Their grandchildren are farmers who tell strange stories about their grandparents.

fail.log: {npc} spits on your cairn and walks away. That was the only answer you were going to get.

events.text: A very small child has come up the mountain alone to gather wild greens, climbed onto your cairn, looked you straight in the eye and asked, "Are you lonely?" Nobody has asked you that in a very long time. {npc} is waiting for an answer, with the patience only very small children and very old beasts have.

choices.text: "Yes"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, then sits down on the cairn and stays until dusk, picking greens and telling you about a dog, a sister, a neighbour's goat. It is the best afternoon you have had in a long time.

choices.text: "No. I have the whole valley"

effects.log: {npc} considers this and decides it is a fib. "I will come back tomorrow," {npc} announces, "in case." And does, for six years.

choices.text: "Go home before it gets dark, small one"

effects.log: {npc} goes, but leaves you half the basket of greens, laid out on the cairn very neatly, as one would for a friend.

events.text: In the hidden valley at the back of your mountain there is a village nobody visits: the lepers, driven out of every town. They grow millet and say nothing to anyone. Today one of them, {npc}, has climbed to the ridge to speak to you, because you are the only being in the province who is not afraid of them.

choices.text: "What does the village need?"

effects.log: Salt, a spring that does not freeze, and someone to frighten off the boys who throw stones. You give all three. The village survives a famine that empties two towns.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the stories of the outside world, for an evening

effects.log: Markets, festivals, a new king, an old scandal. {npc} carries every word back to the valley and tells it for a year. Being forgotten is lonelier than being sick, {npc} says.

choices.text: Show {npc} the herb on the north cliff that eases the pain

ok.log: It does not cure. It eases. The valley gathers it every autumn after, and the old ones sleep through the winters.

fail.log: The cliff has changed since you last looked. The herb is gone. You find a smaller patch, later, and send word.

events.text: A palace coup in the capital. A boy prince has fled with one old eunuch, and they have come up your mountain in the rain because the stories say the mountain shelters the hunted. {npc} is fourteen, soaked and trying very hard to be royal about it. "If you hide me," {npc} says, "when I am king, I will make you a lord."

choices.text: "Do not promise. Just sleep"

effects.log: You keep the rain off the overhang all night and walk the soldiers in circles until dawn. {npc} sleeps like the child {npc} is. The eunuch does not sleep at all, and weeps, quietly, with relief.

choices.text: "I do not need a lord's title. The kingdom needs a kind king. Promise that"

effects.log: {npc} promises, very seriously, the way fourteen-year-olds do. You hide the two of them for a month. Years later, a king rules with a strange gentleness, and says at the coronation only that a promise is remembered.

choices.text: "The quarrels of the palace are not mine." Show them the road out

effects.log: They go on into the rain. You hear later that {npc} reached the coast and a boat. Whether {npc} ever became king, the stories differ.

events.text: A young swordsman from the murim has climbed your mountain to fight you. {npc} has defeated every master in three provinces and needs a greater opponent to break through to the next realm. "I do not want your core," {npc} says. "I want your best. Draw on me."
events.arc: The Swordsman Who Wants a Duel

choices.text: Fight {npc}, at a fraction of your strength

mem.note: fought me at a fraction of its strength

ok.log: For a whole afternoon {npc} fights a mountain and does not lose. Then {npc} understands that the mountain never really fought, and sits down and laughs, and breaks through to the next realm on the spot.

fail.log: {npc} is better than you thought. The sword finds you twice before you knock {npc} off the ledge into a pine tree. Both of you are embarrassed. (-10 health)

choices.text: "Sit down. Your sword is too loud"

effects.log: {npc} sits, sulking, then listening. You teach {npc} for a month how wind moves through a gorge without fighting it. {npc} leaves without having drawn on you once, and comes out of seclusion two years later, unbeatable.

choices.text: Show {npc} your full strength, for one heartbeat

effects.log: One instant of what you truly are. {npc} goes white, drops the sword into the gorge, and goes home to become a farmer. The murim loses a genius. The farm does very well.

events.text: A royal physician has come with a medicine chest, a silver knife and a sick child: the king's own grandchild, with a wasting illness nothing cures. Every old text says the same thing, {npc} explains, mortified: a piece of a great beast, ground and boiled. "Only a little," {npc} says. "I would not ask if the texts gave another way."
events.arc: The Physician Who Asks for a Piece of You

choices.text: Allow it: one small cut

effects.log: The physician's hands shake so much you have to hold still for a long time. The child recovers. You carry a small white scar for the rest of your life, and do not mind it. (-15 health)

choices.text: "The texts are wrong. Look at the child's water and food instead"

ok.log: You have watched generations of human sickness. The child is being slowly poisoned by a lead-glazed bowl. {npc} goes white, then furious, then back to the capital at a gallop.

fail.log: You are wrong about the cause. {npc} goes home with nothing. The child lives anyway, by the luck that sometimes comes.

choices.text: "No. Once one physician takes a piece of me, every physician will come"

effects.log: {npc} bows, understanding exactly, and leaves. You never learn what became of the child. That stays with you.

events.text: A mapmaker has walked the whole kingdom for twenty years with a measuring cord and a pack of paper, making one great map of every ridge and river. {npc} has come to your peak because it is the last blank place on it. "The villages call this mountain a dozen names," {npc} says. "What do you call it?"

choices.text: Give {npc} the true name, the one you have never said aloud

effects.log: {npc} writes it on the map in small careful characters. It is on every copy for generations. Nobody knows how to pronounce it. They say it anyway.

choices.text: "Write: here, something lives. Leave the rest blank"

effects.log: The one blank on the great map of the kingdom, with five characters in it. It does more for your legend than any name could have.

choices.text: Show {npc} the ridges from your height, all of them

effects.log: From up there {npc} sees the whole spine of the land at once and corrects four mountains and a river on the spot. The map is the finest ever made. {npc} weeps at the view.

events.text: An old hunter has climbed your mountain one last time, in snow, very slowly. {npc} hunted on these slopes for sixty years and always knew you were there and never once shot at you. {npc} builds a small fire and talks to the dark: "I wanted to see you, once. Just once. Before the end."

choices.text: Come into the firelight

effects.npcPass: the cold, at peace, by a fire on the mountain
effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long, long time, and smiles, and says, "Yes. I thought so." You stay by the fire until it goes out. In the morning {npc} is still smiling. You bury {npc} under the pines.

choices.text: Speak from the dark, and let {npc} keep the mystery

effects.log: "Hunter," you say, "you were always welcome." {npc} laughs, wheezing, and goes down the mountain the next day content, and dies in bed that spring, telling everyone.

events.text: A potter at the kiln on your lower slope has been trying for twelve years to make a perfect moon jar: a great round white jar, two halves joined at the belly. Every one has cracked in the firing. {npc} has stopped praying to the kiln god and started talking to you. "I do not need it perfect," {npc} says. "I need it whole."

choices.text: Hold the kiln's heat even all night, the way only you can

ok.log: In the morning there is a white jar, slightly lopsided, glowing like the moon at dawn. {npc} sits in front of it for a whole day without speaking. Centuries later it is the most famous jar in the kingdom.

fail.log: It cracks anyway, a fine line from shoulder to belly. {npc} looks at it for a long time and then says, "That is the best one yet," and means it, and keeps it.

choices.text: "Join the halves a little crooked. Whole is not the same as perfect"

effects.log: {npc} stares, then laughs, then goes back to the wheel. The next jar survives the firing, crooked at the seam. {npc} says it looks like it is breathing. It does.

events.text: You count them one evening: the names the valley has for you. The Old One of the Pass. The Keeper of the Road. Grandfather Mountain. The Thing in the Ravine. The Honoured Spirit. The Quiet One at the Spring. Eleven names in eleven villages, and in each village you are a little different. None of them is wrong.

choices.text: Try to be all of them

effects.log: It is exhausting and wonderful. You learn eleven sets of rites and eleven sets of grudges. You are, perhaps, larger than you were.

choices.text: Choose one, and be that

effects.log: You choose the one a child invented, the least grand of all. You find it fits you better than the others, and you grow into it.

choices.text: Be none of them. Be what you are

effects.log: You let the names fall off you like leaves. The villages keep them. You keep yourself. It is a kind of freedom, and a kind of loneliness, and you accept both.

events.text: A young family has climbed to your cairn with a letter so old the paper is brown lace. It was written by a great-great-grandparent you knew: someone you saved, or argued with, or loved, in a way. The letter says: when my family is in trouble, take them to the mountain. They are in trouble. They have come.

choices.text: Help them, as you would have helped the one who wrote it

effects.log: A debt, a cruel landlord, a sick child. You deal with all three, one way or another, over a season. They go home believing in the letter. So do you.

choices.text: "Tell me about your family. All of it, back to the one who wrote this"

effects.log: Five generations, as they tell it. You correct only a few details. The trouble, when you understand it, is small. The story is not.

choices.text: Give them the old one's words: tell them what their ancestor said to you

effects.log: You remember every word. The family weeps to hear an ancestor speak. They go home with no money and no help except that, and somehow it is enough.

events.text: The clouds part one night with no wind, and something looks down: not a god exactly, not an official exactly, but the attention of heaven, the way a farmer looks at a field to see if it is ready. You have changed a valley, spoken to kings, held back armies. Heaven has noticed. It does not say whether it approves.

choices.text: Look back up, and do not lower your eyes

effects.log: You meet it. Something up there seems, very faintly, amused. The clouds close. For a decade afterwards thunder never falls within ten li of you.

choices.text: Bow your head, and wait

effects.log: You stay bowed until dawn. When you lift your head the sky is ordinary. But your qi moves differently afterwards, smoother, as if a door somewhere has been unbarred.

choices.text: Pretend to be asleep

effects.log: Heaven, it turns out, is not fooled, and also does not mind. The clouds close. You lie very still until morning, feeling ridiculous and safe.

events.text: The court has decided you have too much influence: villages that consult a mountain before the magistrate, rites the ministry did not approve. A state exorcist is coming up the path with officials and soldiers and yellow talismans to bind you. Halfway up, the path is blocked by two hundred villagers with their arms linked, who will not move.
events.arc: The Exorcist and the Grand Council

choices.text: Tell the villagers to step aside, and meet the exorcist yourself

ok.log: The talismans burn up one by one as they touch you, like moths in a lamp. The exorcist stands in the drifting ash and, after a long silence, bows. The report to the court says the spirit was found benevolent and beyond binding. Both are true.

fail.deathCause: a state exorcist's binding, met face to face to spare the villagers
fail.log: The binding holds, and tightens.

choices.text: Let the villagers hold the path. It is their choice

effects.log: The soldiers will not strike farmers who are not resisting. The officials argue. The exorcist sits on a rock and waits three days, then goes home and writes that the mountain is protected by the people, which the court finds harder to deal with than a spirit.

choices.text: Speak to the exorcist over the villagers' heads, as one power to another

effects.log: You talk until dark about rites, about ministries, about whose valley this is. The exorcist leaves with an agreement: the rites stay, and are written into the county register, which makes them the court's, which makes everyone happy.
